hint: A square root simplifies when the number inside has a perfect square as a factor. Which perfect squares divide $50$?

hints.text: A square root simplifies when the number inside has a perfect square as a factor. Which perfect squares divide $50$?

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Try an easier radical: $\sqrt{12} = \sqrt{4}\sqrt{3} = 2\sqrt{3}$. Pull out the largest perfect square you can find; the rest stays under the root.
Write $50$ as $25 \times 2$, since $25$ is the largest perfect square factor. Then take the square root of $25$ out in front.
Since $\sqrt{25} = 5$, the result is $\sqrt{50} = 5\sqrt{2}$, which is choice B.

learningObjective: Simplify a radical by extracting a perfect-square factor.
explanation: Write $50$ as a perfect square times another number: $50 = 25 \times 2$.
The square root of a product is the product of the square roots, so $\sqrt{50} = \sqrt{25} \cdot \sqrt{2}$.
Since $\sqrt{25} = 5$, this simplifies to $5\sqrt{2}$, which is choice B.

alternativeExplanations.title: Check with a decimal
steps: Evaluate the choices: A is about $35.4$, B is about $7.07$ ✓, C is about $4.47$, D is about $22.4$.
A quick decimal estimate is a reliable check on any radical-simplification question, and it needs no rules at all.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: Choice A, 25√2, pulls the 25 out of the radical without square-rooting it.
Whatever leaves the radical must exit as its square root: √25 becomes 5 outside. Check by squaring back: (5√2)² = 50 ✓
